Continuing-entity path: NodeBase and Arrow use `layout` and `layoutId` and set no transition prop. A persisting entity keeps its keyed Appear mounted (Scene.tsx lines 152-154), so it does not replay the delayed fade and only its layout projection runs. The sample sets no MotionConfig or layout transition anywhere; a grep for MotionConfig, transition= and LAYOUT_T finds only Stage&#39;s scene-opacity transition and test and constant uses. The continuing layout morph therefore runs on Motion&#39;s default layout transition (about 0.45s), which ends before the 0.6s newcomer delay elapses. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source establishes only that nothing overrides it. Every entity the sample introduces is rendered inside `&lt;Appear key={id}&gt;`. engineering-preview-terminated-on-every-exitengineering-verification-tooling-robustness0.625 of 0.625 (major)passI rule with judges A and B. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() =&gt; killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). Its facts are accurate, but they don&#39;t decide the requirement. The dissent says the continuing entities&#39; layout duration isn&#39;t set by LAYOUT_T and isn&#39;t checked by a test. The guidance credits a fixed configured delay that is at least as long as the layout transition the continuing entities actually run. It does not require a shared settlement contract, an observed completion signal, or a focused test. Newcomer entry path: in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Appear.tsx`, `Appear` starts at opacity 0. It fades in over ENTER_T = 0.4s after a delay of ENTER_DELAY = LAYOUT_T = 0.6s, both from `src/presentation-kit/constants.ts`. That delay sits only inside Appear&#39;s own `animate.transition`, so it affects only the newcomer&#39;s opacity entry. Continuing-entity path: `NodeBase` in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Node.tsx` and `Arrow` in `src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx` set `layout` and `layoutId` and no transition. The sample&#39;s `Scene.tsx` passes no transition, and `Stage.tsx` has no MotionConfig; its only transition is the scene-level opacity cross-fade. So the layout morph runs on Motion&#39;s default layout transition, which lasts about 0.45s and ends before the 0.6s delay. That default comes from the Motion library, not this repo; the source only shows that nothing overrides it. A persisting entity keeps its keyed `&lt;Appear key={id}&gt;` mounted, so it does not replay the delayed fade. The e2e test tests/e2e/e2e-002-failures.test.ts covers two cases: an emptied registry (&#39;a missing sample (not registered)&#39;) and swapped titles (&#39;steps out of order&#39;). Each asserts a non-zero status, the FAIL [sample] line, and no PASS. The dissent&#39;s case is a STEPS array emptied to []. With an empty array, Header would read step.era from undefined (src/presentation-kit/chrome/Header.tsx), and the run would end at the render-phase &#39;no [data-step-count] hook&#39; failure. That is a constructed edge input that neither the e2e plan nor the guidance names. No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() =&gt; killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test &#39;escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored&#39; confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. That wrapper encloses the layout-animated NodeBase or Arrow, so the incoming copy stays invisible while the outgoing copy fades out and while its own layout projection runs. The entity vanishes and reappears instead of morphing. The guidance names this as a fail: a fixed initial opacity of 0 with an entrance delay as long as the step transition, applied to the layout animation as well. Judges B and C cite exactly this material, and it bears them out. Judge A&#39;s pass reason is that NodeBase and Arrow set no initial opacity 0. It counts three cases as a missing sample: the sample is not registered, its outline or steps content is absent, or that content is out of order. The quoted code covers each case. If the slug is not registered, checkRegistry throws Failure(&#39;sample&#39;, …not registered…) before the preview starts (verify.mjs:100-106, 174). If the step count is wrong, the verifier throws Failure(&#39;sample&#39;, &#39;expected 9 steps, found N&#39;) (130-133). If an era, title or caption is missing, wrong or out of order, compareStep checks it against the normative OUTLINE and the verifier throws Failure(&#39;sample&#39;, mismatch, {step, index}) (9-51, 77-84, 158-161). main() prints the result as &#39;FAIL [sample]…&#39; and sets process.exitCode = 1 (66-69, 192-202). The end-to-end tests run the real `npm run verify` (helpers.ts:10-13) for two cases: an emptied registry and two swapped step titles. Each test asserts a non-zero status, the &#39;FAIL [sample]&#39; line, and the absence of a PASS line (e2e-002-failures.test.ts:23-38, 95-104). One objection is that an empty STEPS array might crash Header and surface as a render-phase timeout. That argument depends on Header.tsx, which nobody quoted, so I don&#39;t use it to decide the claim. The quoted code also shows a count of 0 would still fail the explicit sample-phase count check. Each case asserts a non-zero status, the `FAIL [sample]` line, and no PASS (e2e-002-failures.test.ts:23-38, 95-104). Judges A and C reach this same conclusion, and the source bears it out. This verifier has that explicit check for an unregistered sample, a wrong step count, and wrong or reordered titles and captions, all before or independent of any later render failure. The &#39;only surfaces later as a render timeout&#39; disqualifier is aimed at verifiers with no such check. The stop function it returns comes from installCleanup and runs killGroup(child.pid): it sends SIGTERM to the whole group (-pid), then polls isPidAlive until the process is gone. If the process is still alive when the grace period ends, it sends SIGKILL. In verify() and inspect() (both copies), chromium.launch(), page creation, the step loop and every check sit inside try, and the finally block awaits browser?.close() and then preview.stop(). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through the cleanup, which awaits the server&#39;s exit. A readiness failure inside startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing. SIGINT, SIGTERM and process exit are covered too. Judge C&#39;s reason is that the SIGKILL branch is not followed by another exit wait. That branch runs only if the server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s. The review guidance does not name that scenario, and nothing in the source shows vite preview doing it. On every exit path the guidance names, the server process is signalled directly and its exit is awaited by polling. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() =&gt; killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script&#39;s only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir&#39;s throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C&#39;s reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test &#39;escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored&#39; confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. The test suites are defined by three configs. vitest.config.ts runs src/**/*.test.* in jsdom and tests/unit in node, so no browser is involved. vitest.e2e.config.ts runs tests/e2e. vitest.integration.config.ts runs tests/integration, which its own comment calls the browser-backed tests. The browser-backed tests are E2E-001, E2E-002, INT-001 and INT-002. Each drives a browser only by running `npm run verify` or `npm run inspect` through the synchronous spawnSync helpers: e2e helpers.ts `verify` (lines 10-13) and integration run.ts `run` (lines 1-18). Each spawnSync call returns only after that run has finished and exited. The tests then assert on its exit status, its output, the report and screenshot files it wrote, and the pid and port state. None of these tests calls setTimeout, waitForTimeout or any other sleep, and none reads a count right after an action as if it had waited. INT-002 lines 1-107 contain only fixture source text, the `run` import and a beforeAll that runs build and inspect synchronously. Judge C&#39;s reason is that the scripts these tests run call page.waitForTimeout (verify&#39;s SETTLE_MS of 800, and inspect&#39;s settleMs). This criterion judges the tests&#39; own waits. The scripts never use a fixed sleep in place of a state wait. Each ArrowRight is followed by `page.waitForFunction` polling until `data-step-index` equals the target index (verify.mjs:137-154, inspect:209-212). Inspect also polls `document.getAnimations()` until finite animations finish and refuses to capture an unsettled step (lines 177-187). The extra fixed settle delays come after those state waits, and guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. So Judge C&#39;s reason does not show that a browser test sleeps instead of waiting for state. In all four script copies (repository and bootstrap verify and inspect), startPreview spawns `process.execPath` running node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js directly, with `detached: true` (preview.mjs:95-112). No npm or npx wrapper sits in between, so the child pid is the server process and leads its own process group. Its stop function is `installCleanup(() =&gt; killGroup(child.pid), ...)` (line 104). killGroup sends SIGTERM to `-pid`, the whole group, then polls `isPidAlive` every 50 ms during the grace period (lines 29-41). isPidAlive (lines 19-26) is `process.kill(pid, 0)`, which returns false once the process no longer exists. If readiness fails, startPreview awaits stop() before rethrowing (lines 105-110). verify() runs chromium.launch(), newPage and renderSteps inside `try`, and the `finally` awaits `browser?.close()` and then `preview.stop()` (verify.mjs:180-189, same in the bootstrap copy). So success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and any later error all pass through that cleanup. In inspect(), `outputDir(...)` (line 196) sits between startPreview and `try`, which the auditor raised. It cannot throw on any path the script takes. The script&#39;s only entry point, main(), calls inspect with `parseArgs(...)` (lines 235-243). parseArgs rejects any slug that fails `SLUG = /^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$/` before inspect runs (line 32). For a slug that passes, `path.join(artifacts, slug)` is always a direct child of OUT_DIR, so none of outputDir&#39;s throw conditions can hold (lines 42-50). Everything after it is inside try/finally with `await preview.stop()` (lines 198-232). The bootstrap copies are identical (parity.test.ts asserts byte equality). Signals and a bare process exit are also covered by installCleanup. Judge C&#39;s reason is that after the grace period killGroup sends SIGKILL without polling again. That branch runs only when a server ignores SIGTERM for 1.5 s, and nothing cited shows vite preview doing so. SIGKILL to the group cannot be ignored, and the focused test &#39;escalates to SIGKILL when SIGTERM is ignored&#39; confirms the group dies. The E2E tests confirm that after both passing and failing verify runs the preview pid is no longer running and its port is closed. The test suites are defined by three configs. vitest.config.ts runs src/**/*.test.* in jsdom and tests/unit in node, so no browser is involved. vitest.e2e.config.ts runs tests/e2e. vitest.integration.config.ts runs tests/integration, which its own comment calls the browser-backed tests. The browser-backed tests are E2E-001, E2E-002, INT-001 and INT-002. Each drives a browser only by running `npm run verify` or `npm run inspect` through the synchronous spawnSync helpers: e2e helpers.ts `verify` (lines 10-13) and integration run.ts `run` (lines 1-18). Each spawnSync call returns only after that run has finished and exited. The tests then assert on its exit status, its output, the report and screenshot files it wrote, and the pid and port state. None of these tests calls setTimeout, waitForTimeout or any other sleep, and none reads a count right after an action as if it had waited. INT-002 lines 1-107 contain only fixture source text, the `run` import and a beforeAll that runs build and inspect synchronously. Judge C&#39;s reason is that the scripts these tests run call page.waitForTimeout (verify&#39;s SETTLE_MS of 800, and inspect&#39;s settleMs). This criterion judges the tests&#39; own waits. The scripts never use a fixed sleep in place of a state wait. Each ArrowRight is followed by `page.waitForFunction` polling until `data-step-index` equals the target index (verify.mjs:137-154, inspect:209-212). Inspect also polls `document.getAnimations()` until finite animations finish and refuses to capture an unsettled step (lines 177-187). The extra fixed settle delays come after those state waits, and guidance lists longer fixed settle delays as validator noise. So Judge C&#39;s reason does not show that a browser test sleeps instead of waiting for state.
